intro: A natural extension of insert() — add insertAll(List<T> items) to ArrayListMinPQ that inserts every element in the list, then paste this test into ArrayListMinPQTest.java for a point back.
hints: insertAll just needs to call insert() once for each element in the list — a simple loop.
Use a for-each loop over the items parameter: for (T item : items) { this.insert(item); }
The test verifies both that all 3 elements were added (size == 3) and that the heap property is maintained (findMin() == 2 after inserting 5, 2, 8 in that order).

intro: A classic heap-sort preview — add toSortedList() to ArrayListMinPQ that returns a new ArrayList with all elements in ascending order (without modifying the PQ), then paste this test into ArrayListMinPQTest.java for a point back.
hints: Copy the internal list into a temporary PQ, then call removeMin() repeatedly until it is empty, appending each result to a new ArrayList.
Do not modify the original PQ — work on a copy. You can construct a new ArrayListMinPQ and insert all elements from the original, or directly copy the backing list.
The second assertion (pq.size() == 3) confirms the original PQ is unchanged after calling toSortedList().

intro: Extend binary search — add binarySearchLeft(int[] arr, int target) to EfficientSearch that returns the index of the leftmost occurrence of target in a sorted array (or -1 if absent), then paste this test into EfficientSearchTest.java.
hints: Start with standard binary search: if arr[mid] == target, don't return immediately — instead record mid as a candidate and keep searching left (hi = mid - 1).
Maintain a variable 'result = -1'. When arr[mid] == target, set result = mid and continue narrowing the window leftward.
When lo > hi the loop ends — return result. If target was never found, result is still -1.

intro: A direct application of GCD — add lcm(int a, int b) to Euclid that returns the least common multiple using the identity lcm(a,b) = a * b / gcd(a,b), then paste this test into EuclidTest.java for a point back.
hints: LCM and GCD are related by the identity: lcm(a, b) = (a / gcd(a, b)) * b — divide first to avoid integer overflow.
Call your existing Euclid.gcd(a, b) method — lcm is just one line built on top of it.
Divide before multiplying: return (a / gcd(a, b)) * b rather than a * b / gcd(a, b) to stay within int range for typical inputs.

intro: A sibling problem to anagram detection — add canFormPalindrome(String s) to Anagram that returns true if the characters of s can be rearranged to form a palindrome, then paste this test into AnagramTests.java for a point back.
hints: A string can form a palindrome if and only if at most one character has an odd frequency — the same frequency-counting pattern as anagram detection.
Build a frequency map (array or HashMap) exactly as you did for isAnagram, then count how many characters have an odd count.
Return true if the number of characters with odd frequency is 0 or 1; return false otherwise.

intro: Extend n-gram counting — add mostFrequentNGram(Map<String, Integer> counts) to NGramCounting that returns the n-gram string with the highest count, then paste this test into NGramCountingTests.java for a point back.
hints: Iterate over counts.entrySet(), tracking the entry with the largest value seen so far.
Initialize a variable 'best = null'. For each entry: if best == null or entry.getValue() > best.getValue(), update best = entry.
Return best.getKey() at the end. This is a standard single-pass linear scan — O(n) in the number of distinct n-grams.

intro: Comparable in practice — add a static <T extends Comparable<T>> T findMin(List<T> items) method to a new ShapeUtils class that returns the smallest element using compareTo(), then paste this test into ShapeTest.java for a point back.
hints: Use a linear scan: start with items.get(0) as the current minimum, then compare each remaining element using compareTo().
If item.compareTo(currentMin) < 0, update currentMin = item.
Return currentMin after the loop. This is the same logic Collections.min() uses internally — you're just implementing it explicitly.

intro: Extend your sorted linked list — add contains(T item) to SortedLinkedList that returns true if item is in the list, then paste this test into SortedLinkedListTests.java for a point back.
hints: Since the list is sorted, you can stop early once the current node's data is greater than item — no need to scan the whole list.
Walk the list with a pointer starting at the head. At each node: if data equals item return true; if data > item return false (can't be later in sorted order); otherwise advance.
If you reach null without finding item, return false. Compare using compareTo() rather than equals() since T is Comparable.
